title: Welcome to the Era of Second-Screen Reading
text:
T hree thousand two hundred pages into Sarah J. Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series, I became very worried that I was missing something. I had read close to the page-count equivalent of Proust’s In Search of Lost Time , but by the end of the latest entry, A Court of Splintered Harmony , published last month, my head was spinning. All of the human queens were a muddle for me. Had I missed the locations of the three kingdoms with which our heroes were locked in a diplomatic stalemate? And who, exactly, was Bryce?

 Half of all Americans don’t finish even a book a year, and yet millions of people in this country have read the six ACOTAR novels . Over the past few months, as I embarked on the task of joining those millions, I found the series everywhere. Readers wanted to talk about it with me while white-water tubing in West Virginia; a high-school classmate dissected the plot via Instagram DM; the books came up at a friend’s house party and on a bachelorette trip. These friends and acquaintances, along with so many others, have read—or will soon finish— Splintered Harmony (and then await, in January, its forthcoming 896-page sequel, A Court of Forgotten Melody ). Surely, they aren’t as baffled by its swirl of plots and characters as I am.

 I’d set out on my journey through Prythian, Maas’s faerie realm, in hopes of understanding what made both earnest fans of genre fiction and women I had never considered bookish tear through so many pages in so many numbers. I consider myself a close and deliberate reader, and I’m not a snob—I enjoy both fantasy and romance. But all of my attempts to decipher the Maas magic seemed to fail: I’d either work myself up about the incoherence of her society’s rules and history, or I’d bounce off the text altogether, like a kid sliding down the smooth sides of an inflatable castle. That feeling frustrated me—until I realized I’d been reading it wrong.

 There are, undeniably, ACOTAR obsessives—people who know all about the history of Prythian and its courts, and who instantly recognized Bryce Quinlan, a crossover character from another Maas series. Plenty of fans read, analyze, highlight, and speculate on social media. But it seems unlikely that they could make up the majority of the people who bought 1.7 million copies of Splintered Harmony on the day of its release.

 [ Read: Don’t call them trash ] 

 After I’d finished submerging myself in reams of ACOTAR , a different possibility came to mind: The average fan isn’t overly concerned with all these details—and that’s fine, because these books don’t need you to be. They encourage a new kind of reading, more akin to the Marvel Cinematic Universe than the best-selling worlds of J. K. Rowling, James Patterson, or Jackie Collins . They travel differently too: A core of Easter-egg hunters spreads the word to casual fans, who are drawn mostly to the spectacle. Maas’s books aren’t the first blockbusters designed to be flipped through passively, maybe on a beach or with your phone in hand, but the bifurcated readership is noteworthy. You can choose to lock in, or you can sit back and offer up nothing but your presence and passive delight. The second path, I would argue, is more rewarding.

 W e might be at the end of reading, as my colleague Rose Horowitch reported pessimistically in July. The desire—and ability—to consume books for pleasure is dwindling, by many metrics, and scientists warn that phones are rotting our attention spans . In this environment, the success of ACOTAR , a doorstop series with no film or television adaptation, might seem puzzling. It follows a human girl, Feyre, who gets caught up in the drama of the faerie world next door; she initially falls in love with one hunky Fae man, only to leave him and marry the smoldering bad boy she’d told him not to worry about. By the time of Splintered Harmony , Feyre and her two sisters have all been turned into faeries and live in the magical realm. She’s the High Lady of the Night Court alongside her mate, Rhysand, and they have a six-month-old baby. There are ancient rites, magical weapons, and prophetic seers. And there is a fair amount of sex: Since 2015, when the first book was released, the series has become the poster child for the romantasy boom .

 A surface-level way to understand these books’ popularity is to assume that readers are there for the smut; having grown up with fantasy, they’re ready—and eager—for a mature version of it. That’s certainly a selling point, but compared with similar entries in the genre, Maas’s books are fairly tame, with a very high plot-to-horniness ratio. And many of the fans I’ve met will admit, cheerfully, that the sex isn’t all that earthshaking. (The sex scenes are also where Maas shows off some of her most awkward tics; she insists, for example, on calling a character’s orgasm their “release.”)

 Maas, I think, is offering readers something different—a genuinely epic story that goes down like a Netflix binge, one you can half pay attention to and still robustly enjoy. Like the MCU, it sets off enough fireworks to hook distracted readers who couldn’t care less who Bryce is, but unlike, say, Patterson, ACOTAR isn’t propelled by the question of what will happen next. Instead, Maas offers a kind of second-screen reading: rich in detail but low on crucial narration that cannot be missed.

 [ Read: The rise of must-read TV ] 

 I don’t mean to imply that she’s making scenes skippable on purpose. Everything Maas has written suggests that she cares about building and expanding her magical realms, that she’s thought about the origins of Prythian’s kingdoms, and that she intends to resolve some of the series’ mysteries. Nor do I believe that she’s being asked by her editors to whittle down or simplify her lore to boost sales (in fact, the sprawling faerie world just keeps expanding, to the series’ detriment). It’s just that her building blocks aren’t all load-bearing, in part because they seem interchangeable. Men will “growl” their lines of dialogue many times in the series, and a reader’s eyes will barely register it—except at clearly signposted moments (as when Rhysand growls at Feyre, “Don’t bother buttoning up that nightgown”).

 Splintered Harmony frequently mentions Rask, Montesere, and Vallahan, three kingdoms our heroes hope to recruit to their war effort. But the main characters don’t go there; they just partake in a summit held on neutral ground. This fateful conference has the potential to generate tense, plot-heavy moments of court intrigue and diplomacy. Instead, in the Maas style, the reader can lean back and watch the prose float by. For a long chapter, Rhys, Feyre, and their friend Morrigan try to win over a variety of royal figures, all of whom are introduced (with their clothing) at length:

 “Well,” the golden-haired Queen of Vallahan said, her blue eyes as frozen as the icy mountains of her territory. Nestled in her heavy cloak of furs, a braided circlet of gold across her pale brow and tattooed runes running down her long, bony fingers, she cut an imposing figure. Though no weapons adorned her, there was something about her direct gaze, her stillness, that radiated warrior . Perhaps not one who’d fight on battlefields, but one who would kill to defend what was hers. That gaze now fixed wholly on me.

 A few pages later, negotiations have not quite begun. We get a sumptuous description of the fruits our trio have brought to the summit. We linger on more outfits. Things start to heat up; a few barbs are traded. But then a new character is introduced; another outfit needs describing. Okay, time to start negotiating—except now Feyre has a flashback to a character introduced in the first book, and then she’s thinking back to the arc that made up most of the second and third books.

 For the rest of the chapter, gorgeous gowns, creeping magical tendrils, and billowing shadows wash over the reader. Some people will be thrilled by every detail in one character’s tattoos, which may link them to a conspiracy across the courts that fans have theorized about; others will notice that Feyre mentions a species of magical being that connects ACOTAR with Maas’s Crescent City series. But many readers are likely to breeze through the section, secure in the knowledge that they’ll be guided back when it matters. Nothing gets done, really—but Feyre does kick Rhys under the table and he squeezes her knee; these new parents are still very much in love.

 This exemplifies the Maas experience: a firehose of minutiae punctuated by short bursts of action (or, ahem, action). One of the major plot points in Splintered Harmony is that the main characters are icing out Feyre’s sister Nesta. At first, the reason for their fury seems to be a secret Maas is saving for later—until the reader realizes that the events that led to this fracture happened in a Crescent City novel, House of Flame and Shadow . That book is also popular—it came out in 2024 and sold more than half a million copies in the U.S. in six months—but those numbers are dwarfed by Splintered Harmony ’s sales, indicating that most of the people who now own a copy of the new ACOTAR probably haven’t read that previous book. Fittingly, this omission isn’t really an obstacle to grasping the situation; obsessives can track down the earlier novel, while casual fans can, and will, continue turning pages.

 [ Read: Literature is becoming more like a video game ] 

 In a foreword to Splintered Harmony , Maas writes that it is meant to be read as “the opening part” of a “much, much longer book.” A Court of Forgotten Melody , the coming sequel, will comprise parts two and three; the “eventual, concluding piece” will follow in a succeeding book. Yet even for a first act, Harmony is notably uneventful: Attempts at diplomacy are rebuffed; a naming ceremony for the baby goes awry; a fear-entity returns; Feyre’s middle sister, Elain, is caught having a shocking hookup; Nesta learns to teleport. For anyone left confused, an army of podcasters and TikTokers will soon summarize the major points in short, digestible chunks, not unlike TV-show recaps.

 T he goal of Maas’s prose , rich in detail and sheer word count, is to allow you to see these hot faeries in your mind’s eye—even the sex is choreographed so that you can understand exactly whose hands are where. When she uses figurative language, it’s typically a simile (“blue eyes as frozen as the icy mountains”); when she wants to give a character interiority, she stays close to their mind. Feelings are obvious to the characters, and to the reader: In that negotiation scene, Rhys speaks “with enough bite” that Feyre glances over, to see “his power remained harnessed, yet his face showed his disgust and unbridled rage.” Everything is narrated or stage-directed, as in a screenplay, and the sentences move the reader on rollers from one paragraph to the next. You’re able to simply “watch” events unfold.

 This is different from other kinds of writing. Literary fiction typically relies less on description, and works on multiple levels; in part, it asks the reader to be a partner in the work by, say, intuiting offstage events or interpreting metaphors. Best-selling genre fiction, whether by Patterson or Dean Koontz or Harlan Coben, uses utilitarian prose to convey an exciting plot. Popular romance writers offer titillating sexual tension on every page. Maas, by contrast, gives readers a sense of immersion in a deep mythology—without actually requiring them to get their heads wet. Although die-hard fans will be rewarded with secrets and connections, skimmers will enjoy the work too, as they catch up with their favorite characters and ignore much of the rest.

 Publishers and critics confused by the conflicting signals of our culture—declining reading habits, flourishing bookstores—can find a clue in ACOTAR ’s success about what, and how, many Americans are reading right now. Genre alone can’t explain Maas’s sales: A structural shift might be involved. Perhaps consumers, instead of eschewing reading entirely, are picking up books that promise less friction and more, in a word, stuff. Maybe readers simply want what other forms of entertainment have been offering for years—to be carried away on a soaring, magical ride, with only minor effort on their part. And if the winged hero carrying them also happens to be brooding and handsome, that only sweetens the deal.
